newsitem.title: ITALY: Olivetti CEO Caio replaced by Calaninno.
newsitem.headline: Olivetti CEO Caio replaced by Calaninno.

text.p: Italy's crisis-hit information technology group Olivetti said its Chief Executive Officer Francesco Caio resigned Wednesday at an extraordinary board meeting and his place would be taken by Roberto Colaninno.

Colaninno is currently managing director of automotive group Sogefi, owned by Olivetti ex-Chairman Carlo De Benedetti's CIR holding company. He is a long-standing associate of De Benedetti who remains Olivetti's largest shareholder.

An Olivetti statement said Caio's resignation was precipitated by a failure to agree on what powers should be granted to an executive committee made up of himself, group Chairman Antonio Tesone, Rodolfo De Benedetti and Franco Girard.
Colaninno will now join the Olivetti executive committee after agreement has been reached on how these powers should be shared out, the group statement added.
Caio's replacement by Colaninno is the latest twist in a succession of events that have gathered pace since De Benedetti resigned from the Olivetti board on Sept. 3 after 18 years as group chairman.

Panic selling on the Milan stock exchange has wiped nearly 40 percent off the money-losing company's market capitalisation since De Benedetti's dramatic exit and after doubts were cast over the accuracy of Olivetti's financial accounts.
Caio's 76-day reign included his short-lived victory in ousting De Benedetti from the board.

But he alienated many in top management and suffered a blow to his credibility the very next day when Olivetti's director general in charge of finance and auditing, Renzo Francesconi, resigned after questioning the accuracy of the group's accounts.
Tesone, a De Benedetti family lawyer who was appointed chairman two week ago when De Benedetti was ousted, said Colaninno was ideally suited to taking the reins at Olivetti.

"The results obtained as managing director of the Sogefi group, the international experience that he has matured and the human qualities and the stability I know him to be endowed with made him the ideal candidate," said Tesone.

Tesone also told the board that lawyers had been instructed to sue Francesconi "for his groundless declarations and his irresponsible behaviour." Francesconi had spent less than two months at Olivetti after being appointed by Caio.

Former Chairman De Benedetti was reported to be the prime mover behind the ouster of Caio, his former assistant and who had led Olivetti's 41.3 percent owned Omnitel mobile phone consortium to its successful launch late last year.
The upheavals have seen Olivetti shares plunge to record lows as investors dumped the stock in concern over who was running the loss-making group and its real financial position.
The company side-stepped key questions about its business put by market regulators by issuing a statement early on Wednesday giving details of some of its affairs but leaving out others.

When the stock opened Wednesday it rebounded from record lows of 465 lire (30 cents) set on Tuesday and triggered automatic suspension by touching a 10 percent trading ceiling and forging a day's high of 511.5 lire (33 cents). It then failed to resume trade.

Caio, 39, Tesone and De Benedetti are being investigated by magistrates in Olivetti's home town of Ivrea in north west Italy near Turin who suspect the company may have issued misleading statements about its affairs, judicial sources say.
